newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary government pressed on energy price margins.
newsitem.headline: Hungary government pressed on energy price margins.

text.p: Western utilities are up in arms as the government prepares to say how it will distribute its recently announced retail energy price rises among suppliers and distributors.

The government announced two weeks ago retail hikes of 24.5 percent for electricity and 18.8 percent for gas but did not define the margins which would be granted to energy producers and distributors, in which Western utilities invested over $2 billion last year.

On Wednesday, Electricite de France (EDF) said the Hungarian Energy Office had proposed 18.3 percent as an increase in the price at which regional electricity distributors sell on their power. The company, which has stakes in two distributors, described the rise as "unacceptable".

At the same time, Belgian group Tractebel said on Monday it was considering suing Hungary over the government's energy pricing policy which it said prevented it from making a profit on its investment in the Dunamenti power station.
Power workers are also angry over a failure by employers to pay an increase in 1996 equivalent to inflation, currently around 24 percent.

After unions threatened strike action, the state privatisation agency APV on Wednesday offered a one-off bonus equivalent to an extra three percent of their 1996 annual salary in firms in which APV still has a majority stake.

The size of the retail hikes disappointed Western investors, coming on the heels of a cancellation of price rises for October after the rejection of recommendations by the Hungarian Energy Office of increases rumoured to be 39 percent for electricity and 25 percent for gas.

Companies such as Gaz de France and German electricity giant RWE, which bought into the gas distribution network, were promised an eight-per-cent return on investment from January 1997 and have expressed concern that the January hikes would be too little too late to generate such profits.

Tractebel's Tibor Kuhl said that an adequate framework had been set up through legislation and the mandate given to the Energy Office for setting the rules. By rejecting those rules last year and fixing consumer prices before settling all the costs the government had broken its promises, he said.
"The underlying law says you have to analyse the costs and then the end-price, not the other way round," he said.
"We want the government to wake up and come up with a new proposal that abides by the rules."
Prime Minister Gyula Horn was defiant on Tuesday, saying Hungary would win if Tractebel brought a lawsuit.

"The state can be sued. I suppose we would win because the government hasn't broken any laws," Horn said at a monthly news conference, adding that the government had sought to strike a balance between the demands of Hungarian industrial and domestic consumers and those of the investors.
"We undertook to establish cost-proportional prices in the energy sector from January 1, 1997. This has happened," he said. "There is no decision everybody likes."
But political analyst Tibor Vidos says that whether the government is sued or not it has already lost in the game of investor confidence.

"It once promised something contracted it and didn't deliver," he told Reuters. "The energy investors may scale down, they may withdraw, but it is a bargaining process and I believe they will get at least most of what they want."
"The real negative side is that the government has lost its credibility," he said. "It will take a long time before investors will ever believe in any government promise at all."
